newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices tumble as rival exporters undercut U.S..
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices tumble as rival exporters undercut U.S..

text.p: Wheat prices fell to the lowest level for 16-months on Monday as the United States struggled to compete with rival exporters amid talk its supplies were overpriced.
Argentina, Australia and Canada were seen as the major threats to U.S. export prospects and there was also concern that the European Union might get drawn into a price war.
"U.S. wheat is too high priced relative to the EU and especially Argentina," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for Chicago-based grain house FIMAT Futures.
The United States voiced new worries on Sunday that the EU might undercut U.S. farmers and compete head-on for sales by using subsidies.

"We would consider that fairly aggressive," Agriculture Undersecretary Gene Moos said during a visit to Paris. Such a step would force Washington to consider restoring its own subsidies to protect its farmers, he said.
The EU irritated Washington by bringing back limited wheat export subsidies last month after a 16-month pause.
Exporters were seen competing for scant business.
"The buyers are few and far between, they just don't seem to have an appetite," Searcy said.

December futures on the Chicago Board of Trade fell to a low of $4.00 a bushel, the cheapest price for the nearby contract since June 1995. During that period prices have risen as high as $7.50. It closed 4-1/4 cents lower at $4.00-1/2.
Other markets, however, were in a more bullish mood and the Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 commodities rose by 0.52 points to 243.87.
Crude oil futures ended higher in New York, after pushing past $26.00 a barrel, its highest level since January of 1991, as dealers sold heating oil in favour crude.
"There is some rotation of leadership. Heating oil had become overvalued," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group.
Crude oil on the New York Mercantile Exchange for November delivery settled up 13 cents at $25.92 a barrel after rising as high as $26.05.
"Crude is really bullish. You just don't want to stand in front of it," said Bob Yawger, a trader with E. D. & F. Man International Inc.
Traders said volume was thin, with little buying interest for refined products.
November heating oil closed down 0.43 cent a gallon to 73.63 cents while November gasoline fell only 0.02 cent a gallon at 67.92 cents.
"You have a situation where gasoline on a fundamental basis is as undervalued as the heating oil had become overvalued," said Evans.
Gasoline prices have lagged gains in the oil complex which has been in a firm uptrend in recent months propelled by a heating oil prices. Heating oil has been buoyed by record low distillate stocks.
Traders said political pressure on refiners to step up heating oil output may eventually pull distillate stocks up to more bearish levels, resulting in crude taking over price gain leadership.

After a meeting on Friday between U.S. Department of Energy officials and oil executives to discuss the low distillate inventory situation, Tosco Corp. and Petroleos de Venezuela's Citgo, two major refiners, said they would step up distillate output.
Refiners are producing about 1.3 million barrels a day of heating oil and 3.6 million barrels a day of total distillates, according to the American Petroleum Institute (API).
At October 11, total distillate stocks were 17.7 million barrels below a year ago and heating oil stocks were 18 million barrels below a year ago, the API said.
